strengths: Addresses a timely and important question (generalization vs. memorization) for the emerging area of generative modeling of neural network weights, which has largely been evaluated only via downstream task performance.

Comprehensive empirical protocol: examines four representative and diverse methods (Hyper-Representations, G.pt, HyperDiffusion, p-diff) spanning autoencoders and diffusion models, classification and neural field tasks.

Multiple complementary lines of evidence for memorization: weight-space L2 distance/heatmaps, decision-boundary/3D-shape comparisons, error-overlap similarity metrics, and interpolation/averaging analyses—these converge on a consistent conclusion, strengthening the claim.

Goes beyond simply reporting memorization by testing standard mitigation strategies from image diffusion literature (reduced training epochs, model size, dropout/noise regularization) and symmetry-aware data augmentation, showing these do not resolve the issue—this negative result is itself informative and non-trivial.

Extensive and transparent appendices (per-method setup, additional qualitative examples, alternative similarity metrics, intrinsic dimension analysis, storage-efficiency discussion, limitations) that support reproducibility and thoroughness.

The comparison to image diffusion models (Appendix F) at matched dataset sizes, and the intrinsic dimension analysis (Appendix G) showing weight data has substantially higher intrinsic dimension than image data, provide useful additional context for why weight-space generative modeling may be harder.
weaknesses: The paper's contribution is primarily diagnostic/analytical rather than proposing a solution; while a rigorous negative result has value, some readers may find the lack of any proposed mitigation (beyond noting that symmetry-aware architectures 'may' help) limits its constructive impact.

The four studied methods are evaluated on relatively small-scale, narrow settings (e.g., MNIST/CIFAR classifiers, single-category ShapeNet airplanes, small training checkpoint sets ranging from hundreds to a few thousand). It is unclear how well the memorization conclusions generalize to larger-scale weight-generation settings or more diverse downstream tasks/architectures not covered here.

The permutation-augmentation experiment for HyperDiffusion shows that naive augmentation breaks convergence entirely (Fig. 10/18), which somewhat conflates 'symmetry augmentation is insufficient' with 'a specific naive implementation of it fails to converge'—a more careful architecture-level treatment (e.g., actually using an equivariant network) is left as future work rather than tested, weakening the strength of the symmetry-related conclusion.

The novelty/similarity metrics (max error-set IoU, L2 distance, prediction overlap) are reasonable but somewhat coarse proxies for 'generalization' in weight space; the paper does not explore whether more behaviorally meaningful notions of novelty (e.g., functional diversity beyond misclassification overlap, feature-level differences) would change the qualitative conclusions.

The intrinsic dimension analysis (Appendix G) is correlational and the paper explicitly acknowledges it is unclear whether it explains the observed memorization, leaving this part of the analysis inconclusive rather than a strong additional finding.

Some baselines (Gaussian noise addition, weight averaging/Gaussian fitting) used to argue 'no advantage over simple baselines' are quite simple; it is not fully explored whether more sophisticated but still simple baselines specifically tuned to weight-space structure might already achieve similar accuracy-novelty trade-offs, which would somewhat temper the framing of generative methods being uniquely at fault.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important question—whether generative models of neural network weights actually generalize or merely memorize—filling a clear gap since prior work on weight-space generative modeling evaluated only downstream task performance, not novelty.

Comprehensive empirical methodology: the paper studies four representative and architecturally diverse methods (Hyper-Representations, G.pt, HyperDiffusion, p-diff), spanning autoencoders and diffusion models, unconditional and conditional generation, and classification/3D-shape tasks.

Multiple complementary lines of evidence for memorization: direct weight-space L2 comparisons with nearest-neighbor training checkpoints (accounting for permutation/scaling symmetries and autoencoder reconstruction limits), qualitative weight heatmaps, decision-boundary/3D-shape behavioral comparisons, and a purpose-built similarity metric (IoU of misclassified test samples / prediction overlap), giving convergent findings across independent measures.

Well-designed baselines: noise-addition and simple interpolation/averaging/Gaussian-sampling baselines are used to show that current weight generative methods provide no advantage over trivial alternatives in the accuracy-novelty trade-off—this is a meaningful, non-obvious negative result.

Thorough ablations of standard memorization-mitigation techniques from image diffusion literature (training epochs, model size, dropout/noise regularization) and of symmetry-aware data augmentation (permutation augmentation), showing these fail to resolve the issue—useful negative findings that guide future method design.

Extensive appendices substantially strengthen the paper: additional qualitative examples, percentile-stratified analyses, an intrinsic-dimension comparison between image and weight data offering a plausible mechanistic explanation, a direct head-to-head comparison with image diffusion models under matched data budgets, and a check on whether weight generators could serve as inefficient dataset compressors.
Clear writing and figures; findings are reproducible in spirit since the paper documents exact experimental setups (Appendix A) and uses publicly released method checkpoints/codebases where possible.
weaknesses: The four studied methods, while representative, are relatively small-scale/early works (2022–2024) evaluated mostly on toy datasets (MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, ShapeNet airplanes); it is unclear whether the memorization conclusion generalizes to larger, more recent, or higher-capacity weight-generation approaches (e.g., LoRA/diffusion-based generation for larger backbones), which somewhat limits the scope of the claims despite the paper's broad framing.

The paper is purely diagnostic/analytical and does not propose or validate any concrete architectural or algorithmic fix beyond negative ablations; while this is a legitimate and valuable contribution, some readers may view the lack of a constructive solution (e.g., an equivariant architecture actually tested) as limiting the paper's forward-looking impact, especially since the discussion only gestures at graph-based symmetry-respecting architectures without empirical validation.

The image-diffusion comparison in Appendix F (DDPM on Flowers vs. HyperDiffusion) is a useful but imperfect control: different modality, data statistics, and architecture make the comparison suggestive rather than tightly matched evidence that data quantity alone explains the discrepancy; a more controlled comparison (e.g., matching model/data complexity or intrinsic dimension directly) would strengthen the causal claim in Section 4/Appendix G.

The core novelty metric (L2 nearest-neighbor distance in weight space) is a somewhat crude notion of similarity for high-dimensional, symmetric parameter spaces, and although the paper does address permutation symmetry for two methods, residual under-accounting of symmetry (e.g., incomplete permutation search feasibility, other invariances) could affect the precise magnitude of the reported memorization gap, even if the qualitative conclusion appears robust across multiple metrics.

p-diff's setting (batch norm layers only, checkpoints from consecutive steps of the same run) is arguably a degenerate case for testing generalization since its own training data has very low diversity; while the paper acknowledges and analyzes this limitation (Appendix D), it somewhat weakens the fairness of directly grouping p-diff's results together with the other three methods within the main narrative before the appendix clarifies the caveat.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question—whether generative models of neural network weights actually generalize or merely memorize—which has direct implications for a fast-growing line of CVPR-relevant work (weight-space diffusion/autoencoders for classifiers, 3D neural fields, etc.).

Evaluates four diverse, well-known, representative methods (Hyper-Representations, G.pt, HyperDiffusion, P-diff), spanning autoencoder/KDE and diffusion approaches, unconditional and conditional generation, under each method's own official/primary experimental setup and codebase, which strengthens external validity.

Uses multiple complementary and largely independent lines of evidence: (1) nearest-neighbor L2 distance in weight space with permutation/sign-symmetry-aware matching, (2) a principled non-parametric data-copying statistical test (Meehan et al. Zu score) rather than only visual/qualitative comparison, (3) behavioral similarity (decision boundaries, Chamfer distance for 3D shapes, prediction-overlap IoU), and (4) accuracy-novelty trade-off comparisons against simple, well-motivated baselines (Gaussian noise addition, weight averaging/interpolation).

Goes beyond documenting the phenomenon to investigate causes via targeted ablations: dataset scaling (G.pt, Hyper-Representations), model capacity/overparameterization (random-weight memorization test), reduced training length, model size, dropout/noise regularization, and symmetry-based data augmentation—providing a reasonably systematic account of contributing factors rather than a single anecdotal demonstration.

Includes a system-level contrastive experiment with a standard image DDPM trained on matched data sizes, showing that ordinary image diffusion models transition from memorization to generalization as data scales, which sharpens the paper's central claim by highlighting a modality-specific gap.

Extremely thorough appendix (20 pages) with additional visualizations, alternative metrics, robustness checks (e.g., percentile-based sampling rather than only random examples), intrinsic dimension analysis of weight vs. image data, and a practical discussion of whether these generative models could serve as compact storage for checkpoint datasets—reflecting careful, comprehensive experimentation.

Clear writing and figures; claims are consistently tied to specific quantitative or visual evidence, and limitations (e.g., Zu scores not being comparable across methods, p-diff's low training-checkpoint diversity) are explicitly acknowledged rather than glossed over.
weaknesses: The paper is purely diagnostic/critical—no new method or mitigation is proposed or validated; the constructive suggestions (e.g., symmetry-aware architectures) remain speculative and untested within the paper itself (the one direct test, permutation augmentation for HyperDiffusion, actually breaks convergence and does not yield a working alternative).

The four studied methods (2021–2024) are somewhat dated relative to the more recent line of weight-generation work the introduction cites (2024–2025, e.g., Zhang et al., Cao et al., Soro et al.), so it remains unclear whether the memorization conclusion generalizes to newer, potentially larger-scale or architecturally different weight generators; the paper does not attempt to test any of these newer methods.

Ablation scale is limited in places (e.g., only a single 10x data-scaling experiment for G.pt, which reduces but does not eliminate memorization; Hyper-Representations scaling shows no improvement, and the paper does not push data scale far enough to determine whether memorization would eventually resolve, unlike the clearer image-diffusion scaling trend shown for reference).

The chosen novelty/similarity metrics (max IoU-based prediction similarity, L2 distance, Chamfer distance) are reasonable but somewhat ad hoc proxies for 'true' generalization in weight space; the paper does not deeply engage with alternative or more principled definitions of novelty for functional equivalence classes beyond permutation/sign symmetry (e.g., other invariances, or functional-behavior clustering beyond max-similarity/IoU).

Some findings rely on relatively small sample sizes per condition (e.g., 3–20 checkpoints per qualitative example, though partially mitigated by larger quantitative runs in the appendix), and cross-method comparisons of Zu scores are explicitly noted as not directly comparable, slightly limiting the strength of quantitative cross-method claims.

The relevance/fit to a computer-vision venue is indirect: while the underlying models (classifiers, 3D neural fields) are vision-related, the paper's core content is about generative modeling of neural network parameters as a novel data modality rather than vision perception per se; this may be viewed as a narrower fit for some reviewers despite its methodological rigor.
